sentence: What we are being asked is exactly whether there exists a 2–coloring of G (i.e. a function s : Q → {–1, 1}) so that any two adjacent vertices receive opposite “colors” (i.e. s(x)·s(y) = –1).

sentence: It is a standard fact in graph theory that a graph is 2–colorable (or bipartite) if and only if it contains no odd cycles.

sentence: Thus, to show that such a function s exists, it is enough to show that every closed walk (cycle) in this graph has even length.

sentence: Consequently, one can choose an arbitrary “starting vertex” in each connected component and assign it one of the two signs; then, for any other vertex in that component, define s(x) to be 1 or –1 according to whether the length (i.e. the number of edges) of a path from the starting vertex to x is even or odd (this is well–defined because any two paths between the same two vertices have the same parity since any closed path in the graph has even length).
